nonvacuity: Closed explicit example: N=5, fixed units {0,1,2}, positions (0,4,8,-1,-2), fixed outcomes (0,1,2), and the two assignments treating unit 3 or 4. Both nearest-treated sets have one member; both rank-square sums are 2. Independent exact arithmetic verifies the two correlations are 1 and both inclusive tails are 1. No hypothesis is assumed.

Closed explicit example: ten one-treated assignments, conditioning on untreated fixed units {0,7,8,9} leaves the six assignments treating units 1 through 6, with probability 1/6 each. The assignment-independent outcome schedule satisfies NoEffects, NoInterference and FixedOutcomeNull (compiled in scratch/Check.lean). Independent exact moments give distance square sums (5,5,5,9/2,5,5) and outcome square sum 9/2.

The normalized FiniteLaw support is provably nonempty (scratch/Check.lean). A compiled example is the uniform law on Fin 2 with f=(0,1), where L(0)=1/2 and U(0)=1. The five-unit T1 instance witnesses strictness without empty units or zero variances. Exact checks also cover 7,260 small finite-law instances, including ties and zero-mass support points.

A genuine witness is the five-unit T1 experiment with alpha=1/20, observation treating zero-based unit 3, and g the Spearman correlation of the three fixed outcomes with nearest treated-variant distances. It satisfies no interference, has two conditional assignments and positive rank variances, and gives rejection probability 1 > 1/20. The refutation therefore also refutes the canonical printed assertion, without an empty-unit or undefined-statistic witness.

The explicit ten-unit null experiment has six conditional assignments, fixed-outcome square sum 9/2, and positive distance square sums. Actual statistic values -1/sqrt(90) and -5/6 occur at assignments treating zero-based units 1 and 4 and are distinct; the third value is -3/sqrt(10). The generic constant-statistic implication separately has the inhabited example A=Fin 2, Omega=univ, t=0.

For the universal hypotheses take N=10, Omega=tenOmega, S=tenS, obs=tenAssignment 6, Y=tenYnull and g=tenG. The observed membership, conditional nonemptiness and all three null predicates have compiled checks. The explicit varying-statistic conjunct has the genuine two unequal statistics described in T5; it does not assume statistic constancy.

Take the same nonempty ten-unit conditional design. Both tenYnull and the direct-effect schedule Y(i,z)=i.val+treatment(z,i) satisfy no interference in compiled checks. The latter permits nonzero direct effects. The opposite antecedent of fixed-outcome variation is realizable under the actual adjacency alternative: fixed unit 7 has outcome 2 when unit 1 is treated and outcome 3 when unit 6 is treated.

The six-row example has outcome square sum 9/2 and positive distance square sums. The ordering vectors (1,2,1,1) and (0,2,1,1) have square sums 3 and 9/2, respectively. The weak-monotonicity vectors (1,2,3) and (0,0,1) have square sums 2 and 3/2. Independent rational centered moments verify every counterexample and printed-formula value; no zero denominator is used.

For the universal hypotheses use n=2 and a=b=(0,1), or a=(0,1), b=(1,0). Nonconstancy and rank-square sum 1/2 are compiled in scratch/Check.lean; c=1 and c=-1 realize both proportionality signs and the increasing/decreasing cases. The separate weak-monotonicity and six-row assertions use positive-variance explicit vectors.

For the matrix hypotheses use N=2, positions (0,1), and d(i,j)=abs(i.val-j.val); positive off-diagonal distances are compiled. A diagonal unit exists and has d(i,i)=0. The scalar branch has d=1, with inverseSquare 1=4/9 compiled; the divergence antecedent is inhabited, for example B=1 and d=1/3. No conclusion evaluates an included summand at zero distance.

The partition hypotheses are inhabited by F={0}, C={1}, T={2}, U={0,1,2}; disjointness and the union are compiled. The inconsistent large counts occur only inside a negated conclusion, not as simultaneous hypotheses. Each of the four listed natural-number repair quadruples satisfies N=F+C+T; the printed sum and residual were checked exactly.

Take the ten-unit null example with a=tenAssignment 6: its conditional set has six assignments and its uniform p-values are (1,1,1,1/2,1/3,1/3). Compiled checks establish nonemptiness and the null hypotheses. At attainable levels 1/3, 1/2 and 1, rejection probabilities equal the levels; below the smallest attained value the maximum is the explicitly adjoined zero. The two-point nonconstant-law example also exercises the generic finite-law arithmetic.

Compiled instance: N=2, M=1, focal unit 0 and neighbors={1}. Both own-treatment conditional supports are nonempty; E=1/2, E1=0 and E0=1, giving strict inequalities. To realize unequal neighborhood sizes take N=3, M=1, focal 0 with {1}, and focal 1 with {0,2}; expectations are 1/3 and 2/3. Independent exact enumeration checks all neighbor sets of focal unit 0 for N=2 through 7 and every M=0 through N, with empty conditional supports never used as conditional expectations.

The closed adjacency model uses ten actual units with observed assignment treating unit 6. Its observed fixed outcomes are (1,3,2,1); the conditional set has six assignments with nonempty nearest-treated sets and positive rank variances. Independent construction from adjacency counts reproduces psi, theta, all ten observed outcomes, the six distance rows and squared correlations; exactly two of the six values are at most the observed one.

Both parity hypotheses have positive-count instances: C=2, M=1, k=1 and C=1, M=1, k=0 (compiled). The corresponding maximizers are {1} and {0,1}. Independent enumeration verifies the exact maximizer sets for C=1 through 50 and M in {1,2,7}.
